aj matches on equality for all but the last column, taking the most recent time for the last, as a left join with nulls for unmatched rows

An as-of join's 'backward' default is not an arbitrary choice among equals — it's the only direction available in real time, since 'forward' and 'nearest' both require a sample that hasn't happened yet relative to the left row being processed as it arrives.

items.item: A tolerance is not a precision knob that can be turned down indefinitely for a 'tighter' answer — past the signal's own report period, turning it down only converts correct matches into null ones, it can't manufacture data that was never sampled.

at.step: Predict: can a tolerance below the clock offset help?

items.item: Setting a tolerance below a known clock-offset uncertainty is strictly worse than setting it at the offset: every match the tighter tolerance excludes was already within the looser, correct tolerance, so nothing is gained and real matches are lost.

at.step: Reveal: below the offset, nothing helps

items.item: The null-rate-vs-tolerance curve is a diagnostic in its own right, independent of picking a final tolerance value — a curve with a sharp knee at the signal's known report period confirms the join is behaving as expected; a curve with no knee anywhere suggests the assumed report period is wrong.

at.step: Reveal: the null rate against tolerance

items.item: Interpolation's look-ahead requirement isn't a minor implementation detail — it's the exact same boundary that separates a valid backward-looking analysis from a leaking model feature (Chapter 17's training-set leakage), which is why this topic states the identity to the point-in-time feature join rather than treating them as unrelated.

at.step: Reveal: a step vs. an interpolated value, and its cost

items.item: A step approximation isn't 'wrong' in the way a bug is wrong — it's a documented, bounded kind of staleness (at most one report period old), whereas an unbounded or mis-partitioned match has no such bound and is a different class of error entirely.

at.step: Reveal: a step vs. an interpolated value, and its cost

items.item: A partition key for an as-of join is not an optimization — it's a correctness requirement whenever more than one entity shares a timeline; omitting it doesn't fail loudly, it silently returns a plausible-looking row borrowed from the wrong equipment.

at.step: Reveal: the partition key, and what happens without it

items.item: Running the same join in two different engines (DuckDB and pandas) and asserting row-for-row agreement is a stronger correctness check than testing either engine's output against hand-reasoning alone, because it catches a bug that happens to be consistent with one engine's own quirks but not the mechanism itself.

A badly stale match returned with no error is the general failure shape of any as-of join without a tolerance: the join's contract is 'nearest preceding, however far back that is,' and a caller who wants a recency guarantee has to state it explicitly.

Checking two independent engines against each other catches a different class of bug than checking one engine against hand-written expected values: the latter can be wrong in a way that happens to match a buggy implementation, while two unrelated implementations agreeing is evidence about the mechanism itself, not about either codebase.
